newsitem.title: CANADA: Fletcher strike may boost pulp, newsprint.
newsitem.headline: Fletcher strike may boost pulp, newsprint.

text.p: A strike due to begin next week at Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd could last several months and if so, will likely exert upward pressure on world newsprint and pulp prices, analysts said on Wednesday.
Fletcher's two unions announced on Tuesday they planned to go on strike at its three British Columbia mills next Monday, the second strike in less than three years at the company.

After the company and unions both said they were bracing for a long shutdown, analysts said today the strike could stretch several months. Any walkout lasting more than about a month would hurt Fletcher financially and begin to affect world markets, they said.
"We think that this strike could last for as long as four months," CIBC Wood Gundy analyst Don Roberts wrote in a report today.
"Given that Fletcher represents roughly six percent of the North American newsprint and uncoated groundwood (paper) capacity, a long strike could put some pressure on newsprint prices."

Fletcher and British Columbia's Skeena Cellulose, which has filed for bankruptcy protection and shut its pulp mill late last month, together account for an estimated five to seven percent of the world softwood pulp supply, and the closings would likely affect that market too.
"If the strike stretches two to three months, you'll see upward pressure on both newsprint and pulp," said one Canadian analyst who declined to be identified.
Fletcher, majority owned by New Zealand's Fletcher Challenge Ltd, is well positioned to weather the strike with about C$350 million in cash on hand and extra inventory.
A Fletcher spokesman said the company had built up inventories to about one quarter above normal and many of its customers also stockpiled supplies ahead of a possible strike.
Although its earnings would be hit in a long strike, "the company can survive easily for a long time. The unions have made a big mistake picking this (company)," said one analyst.
U.S. daily newspapers had about 41 days supply on hand, which was about average, the analyst said, but publishers who buy newsprint from Fletcher are worried about the situation.
"If they dig in for a long strike, within weeks everybody would be scrambling for newsprint," said Don MacLachlan, an executive at Southam Inc's Pacific Press unit in Vancouver.

Analysts said it was difficult to estimate the impact on Fletcher's earnings from a strike. A brief strike could actually boost earnings in the short run because the company's costs would fall sharply and sales could be sustained by drawing down inventories.

But afterward there would be a fall in sales as production restarted. Analyst John Carroll of Loewen Ondaatje said a strike longer than four to six weeks would clearly hurt the company. "Then it will obviously have very much of an impact," he said.

The affected mills have capacity to produce about 1.7 million tonnes of pulp and paper a year. That equals about 2,600 tonnes of newsprint and groundwood paper, 2,000 tonnes of pulp and 249 tonnes of containerboard a day.
Prices have been rising and pulp now fetches about US$610 a tonne and North American newsprint about US$580 a tonne.

When the talks collapsed on Tuesday, Fletcher's unions were demanding a three-year contract with a five percent annual wage increase and other provisions that would raise the company's labor costs by a further 20 percent over the life of the deal, Fletcher said.
Fletcher was proposing a six percent wage hike over six years, a cash payout of C$1,000 a worker in exchange for moving to a 365-day-a-year operation from 362 days and greater flexibility.
The unions have said Fletcher's demand for full flexibility, which would allow it to shift work among employees of different job classifications, was the main reason for the talks' failure.

The 2,400 unionized workers at Fletcher have been without a contract since April. The unions targeted Fletcher for pattern bargaining and hope to replicate a contract there at other British Columbia producers.
Fletcher class A shares were up 0.40 to 23.20 on the Toronto Stock Exchange today.
((Reuters Vancouver Bureau (604) 664-7314))
